1540:
A batten is a long, narrow, flat strip of a rigid material — almost always wood, though sometimes metal, fibreglass, or plastic. Picture a short wooden plank, then imagine it sliced lengthwise into a much thinner, narrower strip. That strip is a batten.

What makes a batten different from just "a piece of wood" is its specific shape and purpose: it is always significantly longer than it is wide, and it is relatively thin. Its job, in nearly every situation where the word is used, is to hold, stiffen, secure, or support something else.
Where You Will Encounter This Word

The word "batten" appears in several distinct areas of life. Each use is a bit different, but the underlying idea — a slim, rigid strip doing a structural or supportive job — runs through all of them.

1. In Construction and Roofing

This is probably the most common everyday use of the word.

When a house is being built, the sloping wooden framework of the roof is covered not directly with tiles, but first with a layer of thin horizontal strips of wood nailed across the roof frame. These strips are battens. The roof tiles or slates then sit on top of and hook onto these battens, row by row, like teeth on a comb.

So if you ever look at a roof being constructed before the tiles are placed, you will see a grid of wooden strips running across it — those are the battens.

The same principle is used on walls. A wall batten is a thin strip of wood fixed horizontally (or sometimes vertically) onto a brick or concrete wall, and the finishing layer — wooden cladding, plasterboard, or panelling — is then nailed or screwed onto those battens. The battens create a slight air gap and give the outer surface something solid to attach to.

2. In Carpentry: Batten Doors and Joining Boards

You may have seen old-fashioned doors in barns, sheds, or rustic cottages that look like they are made of several vertical wooden planks standing side by side. Because individual planks can warp and separate over time, shorter horizontal strips of wood are nailed across the back of those planks to hold them all together as one rigid surface. Those cross-pieces on the back are battens.

This type of door is literally called a batten door or a ledge and batten door. The battens are the reinforcing strips; they stop the door from twisting or falling apart.

More broadly, a batten can be any flat strip of wood used to strengthen or hold a surface together — to stop it from bending, buckling, or coming loose.

3. In Sailing

Here, battens serve a beautifully clever purpose.

A sail on a sailing boat is not a flat, stiff surface — it billows and curves in the wind. But if it billows too loosely, especially near the trailing edge (called the leech), it flaps and loses its aerodynamic shape. To keep the sail in the correct, efficient curved shape, sailmakers sew a series of narrow horizontal pockets into the sail fabric. Into each of these pockets, a batten is slid — a long, slender strip of fibreglass, carbon fibre, or flexible wood.

These battens hold the sail's curved shape, prevent flapping, and allow the sail to work efficiently. If you look at a sail closely, you will often notice horizontal lines across it — those are the batten pockets, with the battens inside.

A full-length batten runs all the way from one edge of the sail to the other; a partial batten only goes partway in.

4. In Theatre and Stage Lighting

Walk backstage in a theatre and look up. You will see a series of horizontal metal bars or pipes hanging above the stage at various heights, suspended from the ceiling by ropes or motorised systems. These bars can be raised and lowered. Each one of these bars is called a batten.

Lighting battens have stage lights clipped onto them. Scenery battens hold painted backdrops or flat scenery panels. Borders (fabric strips that hide the upper workings of the stage from the audience) are hung from battens too.

In this context, the batten is essentially the horizontal bar from which things are hung above the stage. It is a core piece of theatre infrastructure.

5. In Flooring

When wooden floors are laid, especially over a concrete base, battens are often used as the first step. Thin strips of treated wood (the battens) are fixed to the concrete surface, and then the actual floorboards are nailed on top of them. The battens raise the floor slightly above the cold, hard concrete, allow air circulation, and give the floorboards a surface to grip onto.

Across all of these uses, the word "batten" always refers to a long, narrow, flat, rigid strip, and it always serves a structural, supportive, or organising function. It holds tiles in place, keeps planks together, maintains a sail's shape, supports lights above a stage, and raises a wooden floor off concrete.

The word is practical and workmanlike — you will find it in the vocabulary of builders, carpenters, sailors, and theatre technicians. The moment you hear it, picture a thin strip of material doing a quiet, reliable job of holding or shaping something bigger.
1541:
"Batten down the hatches" means to prepare yourself for a difficult, dangerous, or challenging situation that is coming. It is a call to take protective action before trouble arrives — not after.

Think of it as saying: "Something tough is on the way. Get ready. Protect yourself now."
Where It Comes From (The Literal Meaning)

To truly understand this idiom, you need to picture an old sailing ship out at sea.

Hatches are the openings (like trapdoors) cut into the flat top surface of a ship — the deck. These openings allow sailors to go down into the lower levels of the ship, where the cargo, supplies, and living quarters are stored. In calm weather, these openings are left uncovered so people and goods can move in and out freely.

Battens are long, flat strips of wood or metal.

When a storm was approaching, sailors had to cover these hatch openings with thick, waterproof canvas sheets (called tarpaulins) to stop seawater from flooding into the ship. They then hammered or pressed the battens over the edges of the canvas to hold everything down tightly and securely. This whole process — securing the hatches before the storm hit — was called "battening down the hatches."

So the literal action was: close everything up and lock it down tight before the storm destroys us.
How the Meaning Jumped from Ships to Everyday Life

Over time, as people used more and more language borrowed from the world of sailing, this phrase left the sea and entered everyday conversation. The "storm" stopped meaning a real weather event and started meaning any incoming difficulty — a financial crisis, a tough challenge, bad news, an argument, or a hard period in life. The "hatches" stopped being literal openings in a ship and started meaning your resources, your defences, your plans.

The core idea stayed exactly the same: close up, protect yourself, and get ready before the trouble hits.
The Exact Feeling the Idiom Carries

This idiom carries a sense of urgency and seriousness. It is not used for small, everyday inconveniences. You wouldn't say "batten down the hatches — my coffee is cold." It is used when something significantly challenging, threatening, or turbulent is expected.

It also carries a sense of action and agency. It is not passive. It is a command, a call to do something — to prepare actively, not to simply worry or wait.

Additionally, there is a sense of anticipation built into it. The difficulty has not yet arrived — but it is coming, and you can see it on the horizon. That is the key moment when this idiom applies: the gap between knowing trouble is coming and trouble actually arriving.

Business:
"The economy is heading into a recession. Every company needs to batten down the hatches and cut unnecessary costs."

Weather (where the literal and figurative blur together):
"The forecast says a massive storm is coming this weekend. Batten down the hatches and stay indoors."

Personal life:
"Her parents are coming to visit for two weeks and they always cause drama. She's battening down the hatches."

Politics/News:
"The government is battening down the hatches ahead of the financial report, knowing the figures will be bad."

Spoken warning to a group:
"Batten down the hatches, everyone — the audit team arrives on Monday."
The Grammar: How to Use It Correctly

• The full phrase is "batten down the hatches" — all four words together.
  • It is most commonly used as a command or instruction: "Batten down the hatches!"
  • It can also be used in a describing form: "The team is battening down the hatches." (present continuous) or "The company battened down the hatches." (past tense)
  • The word "batten" here functions as a verb, meaning to fasten or secure using battens.
What Makes This Idiom Different from Similar Expressions

"Brace yourself" — similar, but more about mentally preparing for a shock or emotional blow. "Batten down the hatches" is broader and more action-oriented — it implies taking practical, real-world steps to prepare.

"Hunker down" — very close in meaning. "Hunker down" means to settle in and endure a difficult period by staying put and riding it out. The difference is subtle: "batten down the hatches" emphasises the preparation phase, while "hunker down" emphasises the enduring phase.

"Prepare for the worst" — a plain, direct expression with no imagery. "Batten down the hatches" is more vivid, more dramatic, and more colourful because it paints a picture of sailors in a storm.

"Circle the wagons" — another idiom meaning to come together defensively when under threat. But this one emphasises group unity and defence, while "batten down the hatches" focuses more on individual or organisational preparation.
A Tip to Remember It Forever

Picture this scene in your mind: a small wooden ship, the sky turning black, waves growing tall, and sailors running across the deck, hammering down covers over every opening before the storm swallows them whole.

That image is the idiom. Whenever life presents you with a storm on the horizon — a crisis, a threat, a hard stretch ahead — and you or someone else takes steps to prepare and protect, that is the moment to say: "It's time to batten down the hatches."
1542:
To batter something means to hit it hard, repeatedly, and with great force — usually to the point of causing serious damage. This is the heart of the word. It is much stronger and more violent than simply "hit" or "strike." A single blow is never battering. What makes battering distinctive is the relentless, sustained nature of the action: blow after blow after blow.

Think of someone trying to break down a locked door in an emergency. They don't knock politely. They pound it with their fists, ram it with their shoulder, kick it again and again — that is battering. The door takes repeated punishment until it gives way.
Meaning 1: To Strike a Person Repeatedly and Violently

When the object of "batter" is a human being, the word implies a brutal, one-sided, sustained physical attack. This is the word used in legal, medical, and journalistic contexts when describing serious assault, domestic violence, or abuse.

"He was arrested for battering his wife."
"The attackers battered him until he lost consciousness."
"The victim had been badly battered."

This is a weighty, serious word in this context. It is not used lightly. It implies that the person being attacked was overwhelmed, could not easily defend themselves, and suffered real harm.
Meaning 2: To Strike an Object Repeatedly

You can batter objects too — doors, walls, locks, or anything you are trying to break, force open, or destroy through repeated powerful blows.

"Firefighters battered the door down with an axe."
"He battered the old lock with a hammer until it broke."
"Protesters battered the gates of the building."

A key phrase that comes from this use is "batter down" — meaning to knock something down by battering it. You will often hear "batter down a door" or "batter down a wall."

This is one of the most common ways "batter" is used, and it feels completely natural because nature — storms, wind, waves, rain — never strikes just once. It keeps going, which is exactly the spirit of the word.

"Huge waves battered the coastline throughout the night."
"The hurricane battered the island for six hours."
"The old lighthouse had been battered by storms for decades."
"Fierce winds battered the trees, snapping several branches."

Notice that in all these cases, there is continuous, repeated force being applied against something. The sea doesn't hit the cliff once. It hits it endlessly. That is why "batter" is the perfect word here.
Meaning 4: The Figurative Use (No Physical Hitting Involved)

"Batter" is also widely used in a metaphorical sense, when something is being damaged severely — not by physical blows, but by financial loss, emotional pain, repeated setbacks, or public criticism. The idea of sustained, damaging repeated impact carries over perfectly into these non-physical situations.

"The company's share price was battered by the scandal." (The scandal hit its value again and again, causing serious damage.)

"His self-confidence was battered by years of criticism." (Repeated criticism wore his confidence down, blow by blow.)

"The team was battered by injuries all season long." (Problem after problem kept striking them down.)

"The new government's reputation was battered within its first month." (It suffered hit after hit to its image.)

In all these cases, the structure is the same: something takes repeated, damaging hits from a force it cannot easily stop.

There is one separate and much gentler use of "batter" in the kitchen. To batter food means to coat it in a thick liquid mixture — made of flour, eggs, and liquid — before frying it. This mixture is called batter (the noun), and the act of coating food in it is "to batter" it.

"She battered the fish fillets and dropped them into the hot oil."
"Battered prawns are a favourite at seaside restaurants."
"He battered the onion rings before deep-frying them."

This use has nothing to do with hitting. It simply means: dip the food into the batter mixture and coat it. The word "battered" in a food context (as in "battered cod") is extremely common in British English especially, and simply means the food has been coated and fried this way.
The Word "Battered" — The Past Form Used as a Description

Because "batter" describes sustained, damaging force, its past form — battered — is very commonly used as an adjective to describe something or someone that has clearly taken a lot of punishment over time and shows the damage.

"A battered old suitcase" — a suitcase that has been knocked around so much it looks beaten up and worn.
"A battered face" — a face showing the damage of repeated blows.
"A battered economy" — an economy that has suffered repeated hard hits.
"Battered and bruised" — a very common phrase meaning deeply damaged but still alive and going.

You will also see compound adjectives built on this pattern: storm-battered (damaged by storms), wind-battered (lashed and damaged by wind), battle-battered (worn down by fighting). These are elegant, vivid ways to describe things.
Tone and Connotation — What the Word Feels Like

"Batter" is never a neutral word. Even when used about the weather, it carries a sense of ferocity and relentlessness. It suggests that whatever is being battered is not having an easy time — it is under siege, taking hit after hit, being worn down. The word naturally creates a picture in your mind of something struggling to hold together under sustained assault.

Compare it to similar words: "hit" is neutral and describes a single action. "Beat" is stronger. "Pound" is very strong and rapid. "Batter" is in the same territory as pound — relentless, forceful, repeated — but with an even stronger sense of damage and overwhelm.
Summary of All Uses at a Glance

"Batter" in every non-cooking sense always means: repeated, forceful impact that causes damage. Whether the thing doing the battering is a pair of fists, ocean waves, a hurricane, a financial crisis, or years of criticism — the word always paints a picture of something being hit hard, over and over, until it breaks, weakens, or suffers visible harm.

In the kitchen, it means something completely separate: to coat food in a liquid flour mixture before frying.

Master those two tracks — the violent/forceful one and the culinary one — and you have complete command of this word.
1543:
Battered describes something — or someone — that has taken a lot of rough, damaging treatment and shows clear signs of it. The single most important thing to understand about this word is that the damage isn't from one quick accident. It comes from repeated blows, long exposure to harsh conditions, or sustained rough handling over time. The word always paints a picture of visible, accumulated wear or harm.

Outside of one specific cooking sense (which we'll cover), battered always feels heavy and a little sad. It is a stronger, more expressive word than simply "damaged" or "old."

1. Physically Damaged Objects

This is the most everyday use. When an object is battered, it means it has taken a lot of physical punishment — it's dented, scratched, torn, or misshapen from years of rough use or harsh treatment. It doesn't just look old; it looks like it has been through a fight.

Examples:

  • A battered old suitcase — covered in dents and scratches from years of travel
  • A battered car — the kind with dents all over its body from years of rough driving
  • A battered book — with a torn cover, bent pages, and a broken spine
  • A battered hat — squashed out of shape from being worn for decades

An important nuance: "battered" often carries a hint of a back-story. When you call something battered, you're implying it has a history — that it has lived through a lot. This is why writers sometimes use the word deliberately to add character to an object. A "battered old guitar" feels richer and more soulful than a "damaged guitar."

2. A Person Who Has Been Physically Beaten

When used to describe a person, "battered" means they have been hit or physically harmed — usually repeatedly. This is a very serious and emotionally heavy use of the word.

  • "He came home from the brawl looking completely battered." — meaning bruised, cut, and beaten up
  • A battered woman or battered wife — a woman who has been subjected to ongoing domestic violence

This sense is so strongly associated with victims of repeated physical violence that it gave rise to serious legal and psychological terms like "Battered Woman Syndrome" — a recognized condition describing the psychological effects of long-term domestic abuse on a victim.

So when you see "battered" applied to a person in a serious context, treat it with gravity. It's rarely used lightly.

3. Emotionally or Mentally Worn Down

"Battered" can also describe a person's inner emotional state — not physical injury, but the feeling of being worn down by life, stress, failure, or hardship.

  • "After months of rejection, she felt battered and hopeless."
  • "The team was battered by the string of losses." (not physically hurt, but emotionally crushed)
  • "His confidence was battered by years of harsh criticism."

Here, the logic is the same: just as a physical object gets battered from repeated blows, a person's spirit, confidence, or heart can get battered from repeated emotional hits.

4. Places or Things Beaten by Weather or Force

This is extremely common. When a storm, hurricane, waves, or any powerful natural force repeatedly strikes a place or thing, we say it was battered.

  • "The coastline was battered by the hurricane for three days."
  • "The small boat survived the battered crossing of the rough sea."
  • "A battered fishing village" — one that has endured decades of storms

The word works perfectly here because storms aren't a one-second event; they pound and lash repeatedly, and "battered" captures that repeated, relentless quality.

5. Food: Coated in Batter and Fried (Completely Different Meaning!)

This is the one meaning that has nothing to do with damage, harm, or hardship. In cooking, battered simply means food that has been coated in batter — a thick liquid mixture of flour, eggs, and milk or water — and then deep-fried.

  • Battered fish — the heart of the famous British dish "fish and chips"
  • Battered onion rings
  • Battered chicken

This meaning is entirely separate from all the others. It's named after a different word ("batter" as in the cooking mixture). So if you see "battered" in a restaurant menu or a recipe, don't worry — nothing has been hurt. It just means fried in a crispy coating!

The simplest way to tell the two apart: if "battered" comes before a food item, it's about cooking. In any other context, it carries the idea of damage or hardship.
How "Battered" Feels Compared to Similar Words

Understanding a word fully means knowing how it differs from its neighbors:

Damaged is a general, neutral word. It simply means something is not in perfect condition. It carries no emotion. A "damaged table" could have a small chip. A "battered table" has clearly been through something — it's visibly beaten up, with a story behind it.

Worn suggests gradual fading or thinning from regular use — like a worn carpet or a worn pair of shoes. It's gentle. "Battered" is not gentle. It implies harsher, more violent treatment.

Broken means something has actually come apart or stopped functioning. A broken vase is in pieces. A battered vase is dented and scarred but still whole. "Battered" describes surviving damage, not complete destruction.

Beat-up is an informal, casual version of "battered" and means essentially the same thing for objects and people. "Battered" is more formal and more emotionally weighty.
The One Feeling That Ties It All Together

Across almost every non-cooking use, "battered" carries a consistent emotional weight. It whispers: this has been through a lot. It has endured repeated punishment. It is still here — but you can see every bit of what it has been through. There's something both tough and sad in the word at the same time.

This is why writers love it. "A battered old lighthouse standing against the sea" tells you far more about that lighthouse's character than "an old lighthouse." The word does double duty — it describes physical condition and implies a whole history of endurance.

1544: The word battery has several distinct meanings depending on the context. Each meaning is used in everyday life, law, military settings, or sports. Here is a thorough look at all of them.

This is the meaning most people think of first. A battery is a device that stores chemical energy and converts it into electrical energy when needed. Inside a battery, chemicals react with each other in a way that pushes electrons through a circuit, producing electric current.

Every battery has two terminals — a positive end (+) and a negative end (−). When you connect a battery to a device (like a torch), electrons flow from the negative end, through the device, and back to the positive end. This flow of electrons is what powers the device.

Two main types:

  • Non-rechargeable batteries (also called primary batteries): These are used once and thrown away when the chemicals run out. The AA, AAA, C, D, and 9V batteries you buy in a shop are examples.
  • Rechargeable batteries (also called secondary batteries): These can be charged and discharged many times. The battery in your phone, laptop, electric car, and wireless headphones is rechargeable. Lithium-ion batteries are the most common type today.

A note on "cell" vs. "battery": Technically, a cell is a single electrochemical unit, and a battery is a collection of cells connected together. However, in everyday language, even a single AA cell is called a "battery," and that usage is perfectly accepted.

Examples of batteries in the world around you:

  • The flat rectangular battery inside a smartphone
  • The large battery pack under the floor of an electric vehicle
  • A 9-volt battery used in smoke detectors
  • A car's lead-acid battery, which starts the engine

In law, battery means the intentional and unlawful physical contact with another person without their consent. It does not require serious injury — even an unwanted touch can legally count as battery if it is done intentionally and is harmful or offensive.

For example, if someone walks up to you and slaps you, that is battery. If a doctor performs surgery on you without your consent, that could also be considered battery under the law.

You may have heard the phrase "assault and battery." These are actually two separate things:

  • Assault is threatening someone or making them fear that they are about to be physically harmed.
  • Battery is the actual physical contact that follows.

In everyday speech, people often use "assault" to mean both, but in strict legal terms, battery is specifically the physical act, not just the threat.

In military contexts, a battery is a group of artillery weapons — such as cannons, howitzers, or rocket launchers — that operate together as a unit under a single commander.

Think of it like a team. Just as soldiers in infantry are grouped into squads, platoons, and companies, artillery soldiers are grouped into batteries. A battery typically consists of several guns or launchers, the soldiers who operate them, and supporting equipment.

Example: "The artillery battery opened fire from the hilltop."

A battery in this sense is roughly equivalent to a company in size — usually around 100–200 personnel.

The word can also refer to a fixed installation of heavy guns, such as a coastal defense battery (a row of large guns built along a coastline to defend against enemy ships).
4. A Group or Series of Similar Things

Used more broadly, battery can mean a set or collection of similar things used together, especially for a common purpose. This use is borrowed from the military sense of guns lined up together.

You will often hear this in phrases like:

  • "A battery of tests" — a large set of tests given together, such as a medical battery of tests (blood test, urine test, imaging scans, etc.) or a psychological battery of assessments.
  • "A battery of questions" — a rapid, extensive series of questions asked one after another.
  • "A battery of lawyers" — a team of several lawyers working together.

The key idea is many of the same thing, all working together or applied in sequence.

In baseball, the word battery refers specifically to the pitcher and the catcher together, considered as a pair. These two players work in close coordination — the pitcher throws the ball, and the catcher signals what pitch to throw and catches it. Because they function as a unit, they are called the battery.

Example: "The starting battery for tonight's game is their ace pitcher and veteran catcher."

Although these meanings seem unrelated on the surface, they share an underlying idea of things grouped or combined to deliver force or power. Multiple artillery guns lined up together deliver firepower; multiple electrochemical cells connected together deliver electrical power; a group of tests or questions delivers a thorough examination all at once. The legal meaning follows a different path but is part of the same word's rich history in English.

1545:
When you describe someone as battle-hardened, you mean they have become tough, experienced, and unshakeable because they have been through many difficult, dangerous, or painful situations — and those experiences have permanently changed them for the stronger.

Think of it this way: imagine a piece of raw metal. It starts out soft and bendable. But when you put it through extreme heat, hammer it, and forge it repeatedly, it becomes hard, strong, and resistant to damage. A battle-hardened person is exactly like that — life (or war, or struggle) has forged them into someone who is difficult to break.

The word has two parts working together:

  • Battle — a fight, a war, or any severely difficult challenge
  • Hardened — made tough and resistant; no longer soft or easily hurt

Together, they describe someone who has been made tough by going through battles. The key idea is that the difficulty changed them. They didn't just survive — they were transformed by the experience into something stronger.
What It Really Means (The Full Picture)

When someone is battle-hardened, several things are true about them at once:

1. They have real, deep experience.
Not the kind of experience you get from reading about something in a book. They have been in the middle of it — the chaos, the danger, the pressure — many times. They know what it actually feels like.

2. They don't panic or break easily.
Because they have already seen the worst, very little can shock or overwhelm them. Where a less experienced person might freeze or fall apart under pressure, a battle-hardened person stays calm and keeps functioning. Their nerves have been tested so many times that they are now steady.

3. They have developed sharp instincts and skill.
Repeated exposure to hard situations teaches you things that nothing else can. A battle-hardened person has learned what works, what doesn't, and how to make good decisions quickly — often without even having to think too hard about it.

4. They carry the marks of their struggles.
This is subtle but important. Being battle-hardened doesn't mean the person escaped without cost. It means the difficulty left its mark on them, but instead of destroying them, those marks became a source of strength. They carry the weight of experience.

In its literal sense:

The word was originally used to describe soldiers who had fought in many wars or battles. A battle-hardened veteran, for example, is a soldier who has seen combat many times, has survived great danger, and has become a formidable, disciplined, and emotionally tough fighter because of it. They are harder to kill, harder to break, and far more capable than a new recruit.

In its figurative sense (very common):

Today, the word is used far beyond war. It can describe anyone who has been made tough and capable by going through a lot of hardship in any field of life.

For example:

  • A battle-hardened politician has survived countless scandals, elections, and crises — and has learned how to handle each one without falling apart.
  • A battle-hardened entrepreneur has seen businesses fail, made big mistakes, lost money, and bounced back — and is now much harder to knock down.
  • A battle-hardened nurse has worked through years of emergencies, grief, and exhaustion — and can now handle the most intense situations with professionalism and composure.
  • A battle-hardened sports team has played through many high-pressure matches and come out knowing how to win under stress.

In every case, the meaning is the same: difficulty has made this person or group stronger, tougher, and more capable.

Battle-hardened is generally a word of respect. When you call someone battle-hardened, you are not criticizing them. You are acknowledging that they have been through a great deal and have come out stronger for it. It carries a sense of admiration for their resilience and experience.

However, it can sometimes carry a slightly heavy or serious tone — it reminds you that the toughness didn't come for free. It came from hardship, struggle, and survival. There is often an unspoken acknowledgment that the journey was not easy.

It's important to be clear about what battle-hardened does not mean:

  • It does not mean cruel or heartless. A battle-hardened person is not necessarily cold or emotionless. They are resilient, which is different from being unfeeling.
  • It does not simply mean "old" or "experienced." A person can be old and experienced but never truly tested. Battle-hardened specifically implies that the experience came through struggle and difficulty, not just the passage of time.
  • It does not mean aggressive or violent. It describes the effect that hard experience has had on a person — not their personality or behavior.
A Simple Way to Remember It

If you ever want to recall this word's meaning quickly, just remember this image:

A soldier who has survived many wars is not the same person they were before the first battle. The wars changed them — made them tougher, calmer, sharper, and harder to defeat. That is what battle-hardened means.

Then take that same idea and apply it to any area of life — business, sports, politics, medicine — and you have the full meaning of this word.
1546: A battleground is a place — or a situation — where a serious, intense conflict takes place between two or more opposing sides. The word captures the idea of a contested space: somewhere that opposing forces are fighting over, competing for, or struggling to control.

In its most direct, physical sense, a battleground is a piece of land where an actual battle is fought or was fought. Think of the open fields, hills, or beaches where armies historically clashed — those are battlegrounds. Gettysburg, Normandy, and Waterloo are all famous historical battlegrounds.

Example sentences:

  • "The soldiers advanced across the battleground."
  • "The museum was built on the site of an ancient battleground."
The Figurative Meaning (Far More Common in Everyday Use)

Here is where the word really comes alive in modern English. A battleground doesn't have to involve armies, weapons, or physical violence at all. It is very frequently used to describe any intense conflict, debate, or struggle — even completely non-violent ones.

Whenever a topic, issue, place, or situation becomes the center of a fierce, serious disagreement between two sides, it can be called a battleground.

Examples of figurative use:

  • "Healthcare has become a major political battleground." — meaning politicians are fighting intensely over healthcare policy.
  • "The courtroom was a battleground for the two rival lawyers." — meaning the legal case involved fierce, high-stakes opposition.
  • "Their divorce turned their home into a battleground." — meaning the household became a place of constant, bitter conflict.
  • "Climate change is a cultural battleground." — meaning people are deeply divided and fighting hard over it.

The key thing to notice is that the word battleground brings a sense of high stakes and intensity. You wouldn't use it to describe a small, minor disagreement. It's reserved for conflicts that feel serious, significant, and hard-fought.
A Very Important Special Use: "Battleground State"

In American politics, you will very often hear the phrase battleground state (also called a swing state). This refers to a US state where both major political parties — the Republicans and the Democrats — have a genuine, roughly equal chance of winning during an election. Neither side has a guaranteed victory, so both fight very hard to win those states. States like Pennsylvania, Michigan, and Wisconsin are often called battleground states during presidential elections.

This usage perfectly illustrates the figurative meaning: it's a "place" (a state) that is being intensely "fought over" (competed for) between two sides.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Battleground vs. Battlefield
These two words are close in meaning, but there's a subtle difference. Battlefield is almost always used in a literal, military sense — it refers to the physical place where soldiers fight. Battleground, on the other hand, is used both literally and figuratively, and in everyday modern English, the figurative use is actually more common. You'd rarely say "climate change is a battlefield," but you'd comfortably say "climate change is a battleground."

Battleground vs. Warzone
A warzone specifically describes a geographic area where active, widespread war is happening right now. It implies ongoing, large-scale, and dangerous military conflict. A battleground is more flexible — it can describe a specific site of past or present conflict, and it can be figurative.

Battleground vs. Arena
An arena also refers to a place of competition or conflict, but it's a much broader, more neutral word. You can talk about "the political arena" without implying intense hostility. A battleground, however, always carries a strong sense of fierce opposition and struggle.
The Feeling and Connotation of the Word

When someone uses the word battleground, they are signaling that:

  1. Two or more sides are in serious opposition. This is not a friendly debate — it's a real, intense conflict.
  2. Something important is at stake. You fight on a battleground because winning or losing matters greatly.
  3. The outcome is not settled. A battleground is an active or contested space — neither side has won yet, or the conflict is ongoing.

The word carries a sense of urgency, struggle, and gravity. It raises the emotional weight of whatever topic it describes.

AspectDetail

To put it simply: a battleground is any place or situation — real or abstract — where a serious, intense conflict is happening or has happened between opposing sides. In literal use, it's a place of military battle. In figurative use (which is very common), it's any topic, issue, or situation where two sides are fighting hard, and where the stakes feel high. The word always suggests intensity, importance, and opposition.

A battlement is a defensive wall structure built along the very top edge of a castle, fort, or tower. It looks like a row of alternating raised blocks and open gaps — like a crown with square teeth, or like the top edge of a chess rook (the castle piece).

The raised solid blocks protect soldiers standing behind them. The open gaps allow those same soldiers to peek out, fire arrows, pour boiling oil, or throw stones down at attackers — without fully exposing themselves to enemy fire.
Its two parts

A battlement has two distinct parts, and knowing both gives you a complete picture:

1. The Merlon — This is the raised, solid block. It acts as a shield. A soldier stands behind it for protection. Merlons are typically taller than a person's torso, so they cover the body well.

2. The Crenel (also called an embrasure) — This is the open gap between two merlons. A soldier steps into a crenel to attack, then steps back behind a merlon to take cover. The term crenellations (or crenels) is sometimes used as a synonym for battlements as a whole, because the gap-and-block pattern is their most defining feature.

You can remember it this way: merlon = the wall, crenel = the hole.
Where you find battlements

Battlements appear:

  • Along the top of outer castle walls (called the curtain wall)
  • Around the top of towers and keeps
  • On the edges of fortified bridges and gatehouses
  • On city walls of medieval towns

The walkway or platform just behind the battlements — where soldiers actually stood and patrolled — is called the wall-walk or allure. A soldier standing on the wall-walk could duck behind a merlon, then lean into a crenel to fight.
Why they were built that way

The alternating pattern was not random. It was a precise tactical design:

  • The spacing was wide enough for a soldier to shoot through comfortably, but narrow enough to make him a difficult target.
  • The height of the merlons was calibrated to protect a standing person's head and chest.
  • The depth (thickness) of the wall below gave archers room to draw their bows fully before stepping into the gap.

Early battlements were open at the top of the crenel. Later designs added shutters (hinged wooden flaps) over the crenels, which a soldier could swing open to shoot, then close for cover.

Some merlons also had narrow vertical slits cut into them — called arrow loops or loopholes — so a soldier didn't even need to step into the exposed gap to fire. He could shoot through the slit while remaining almost fully hidden behind solid stone.
A further refinement: Machicolations

More advanced battlements sometimes included machicolations — floor openings that projected outward from the wall just below the battlement level. Through these holes, defenders could drop stones, boiling water, or burning material directly downward onto attackers who had reached the base of the wall. Think of it as a built-in trapdoor aimed straight down at anyone trying to climb or break through.
Battlements as a symbol of power and authority

In medieval Europe, having battlements on your building was not just a military matter — it was a legal and social one. In England, for instance, a lord had to obtain a royal license (licence to crenellate) before he could add battlements to his home. This was because battlements signified military fortification and power, and the king wanted to control who could display that kind of strength.

As a result, battlements became a status symbol. Even buildings with no real military need — manor houses, churches, abbeys — were given battlements purely to project authority and prestige.
Battlements as pure decoration

By the late medieval period, and even more so during the Gothic Revival of the 18th and 19th centuries, battlements lost most of their military function and became almost entirely decorative. Architects added them to mansions, universities, churches, and public buildings purely for their dramatic, historical look — to evoke the grandeur of the medieval past.

Today, you'll still see battlements on:

  • Old university buildings (Oxford, Cambridge, and many others)
  • Gothic-style churches
  • Some older government buildings and courthouses
  • Theme parks and castles built for tourism

In these contexts, the battlement is purely aesthetic — no soldier will ever stand behind those merlons.
In everyday language and literature

The word battlement also appears figuratively in writing and speech to describe anything that feels defensive, imposing, towering, or fortress-like. A poet might describe a cliff face as having "natural battlements," or a writer might describe a stern, closed-off person as hiding "behind the battlements of their pride." The image it conjures is always one of guarded height — something raised up and bristling with defense.
Battlement vs. related words — quick clarity

These words often appear alongside battlement, and it helps to know how they differ:

  • Parapet — A low protective wall at the edge of any elevated surface (a bridge, a roof, a cliff path). A battlement is a type of parapet — specifically the crenellated (gap-and-block) kind. All battlements are parapets, but not all parapets are battlements.
  • Crenellation — Either a single crenel (gap), or the overall system of battlements on a wall. Often used interchangeably with battlement.
  • Rampart — The broad, thick bank of earth or stone that forms the main body of a fortification. Battlements sit on top of ramparts.
  • Turret — A small tower projecting from a wall or corner. Turrets often have their own battlements at the top.
  • Keep — The main central tower of a castle. Its top is typically lined with battlements.
In a sentence — natural usage examples

• The soldiers crouched behind the battlements as arrows rained down on the castle walls.
  • The old cathedral had stone battlements running along its roof, though they had never seen a battle.
  • From the battlements, the guards could see the entire valley spread out below them.
  • The architect designed the mansion with decorative battlements to give it a grand, medieval appearance.
Summary in one sentence

A battlement is the row of alternating raised blocks (merlons) and open gaps (crenels) built along the top of a castle or fortified wall, designed to protect soldiers while allowing them to attack enemies from above.

The core meaning. "Batty" means slightly crazy, eccentric, or foolish in a mild, harmless way. It's an informal word used in everyday speech to describe someone whose thinking or behavior seems a little odd, irrational, or out of touch with common sense.

Not full-on madness. Think of "batty" as a gentle shade of crazy — not dangerous insanity, but the quirky, harmless kind. A batty person might believe strange things, say things that don't quite add up, or behave in a way that baffles others — but they're not a serious threat to anyone. The word almost always carries a tinge of humor or even warmth with it.

Who or what can be "batty"? It can describe a person ("My neighbor is a bit batty — she knits sweaters for her goldfish"), an idea or plan ("That's a completely batty scheme!"), or someone's behavior in general ("He's been acting batty all week"). Notice how a bit batty is an extremely common pairing — the phrase softens the meaning even further, making it sound almost affectionate.

Tone — fond, not cruel. This is one of the most important things to understand about this word. "Batty" is rarely a serious insult. It usually sounds warm or gently teasing. When you call someone batty, you're more likely chuckling at their oddness than genuinely attacking them. People often use it lovingly to describe a quirky elderly relative or a charmingly absent-minded friend.

"Go batty." This is a very natural and common phrase. If someone went batty or is going batty, it means they started losing their mind or acting irrationally — often because of stress, monotony, or a frustrating situation. For example: "Being stuck inside all day made me go completely batty." It can also simply mean you were driven to exasperation by something or someone.

Informal only. "Batty" is a casual, conversational word. You would never use it in formal writing, a professional email, or academic work. It belongs purely in spoken language or relaxed, informal writing.

British flavour. The word is significantly more common in British English than American English. If you're in an American context, people are more likely to say nutty, loopy, wacky, or kooky to mean the same thing. That said, "batty" is broadly understood across the English-speaking world, so you won't confuse anyone by using it.

How it compares to similar words. Words like nutty, loopy, dotty, daft, crackers, dippy, and kooky all share the same informal, lighthearted sense of mild craziness. Of these, dotty is the closest cousin to "batty" in tone and feel — both are gently British, both suggest harmless eccentricity rather than serious mental instability.

One thing to watch out for. In some varieties of English — particularly Jamaican and Caribbean English — "batty" is used as a noun referring to the buttocks. This is a completely unrelated usage. Just be aware that if you ever hear "batty" used as a noun in those regional contexts, it means something entirely different.
1549: A bauble is a small, shiny, decorative object that looks attractive but has little or no real value. Think of something that catches your eye, maybe even makes you say "oh, pretty!" — but when you pick it up and think about it, it's essentially worthless. Cheap, trivial, but eye-catching. That is the soul of a bauble.

1. A cheap, showy trinket or ornament

This is the broadest and most fundamental meaning. A bauble is a small decorative item — like a glittery brooch, a sparkly charm, a gaudy little figurine, or any bit of cheap jewelry — that has more flash than substance. The key combination is: looks fancy, isn't worth much.

Imagine a market stall covered in shiny little objects: plastic gems, fake-gold pendants, tiny colourful objects. Those are baubles. They dazzle at first glance but have no real worth.

2. A Christmas tree ornament (especially in British English)

In everyday modern British usage, a bauble most commonly refers to those round, shiny balls you hang on a Christmas tree — the hollow spheres made of glass or plastic, often in red, gold, silver, or other bright colours, that reflect light and make the tree look festive. If a British person says "we hung baubles on the tree," they mean these decorations.

This usage fits perfectly with the word's core meaning: Christmas baubles are visually appealing and festive, but each one individually is a trivial, inexpensive little thing.

3. A jester's mock scepter (historical)

In older, historical usage, a bauble referred to the short stick or mock-scepter carried by a court jester (the professional fool who entertained royalty in medieval times). This stick was typically decorated with a carved head, ribbons, or bells, and it was a prop of foolishness and comedy. It was called a bauble because — just like a shiny trinket — it looked like a symbol of power (a real king carries a scepter), but it was actually a silly, meaningless object meant to mock the very idea of importance.

You're most likely to encounter this meaning when reading older literature, Shakespeare, or historical texts. It's not a common everyday usage today.
The Tone and Feeling of the Word

Here's something important: bauble carries a slightly dismissive or condescending tone. When someone calls something a bauble, they're not just saying it's decorative — they're subtly suggesting it's frivolous, trivial, or not worth taking seriously.

The word implies a kind of surface-level sparkle that hides a lack of real depth or importance. It's the verbal equivalent of rolling your eyes at something flashy.

Because of this dismissive tone, bauble is also used figuratively to describe anything — not just a physical object — that seems impressive or valuable but is actually trivial or meaningless.

For example:

  • A critic might call a prestigious-but-empty award "a mere bauble" — meaning it looks impressive but doesn't really signify anything worthwhile.
  • Someone could dismissively say a politician's achievement is "just a bauble" — meaning it's a shiny, feel-good thing with no real substance.

In this figurative sense, you could apply the word to titles, honours, achievements, possessions, or anything else you want to suggest is more flashy than meaningful.

• "She came home from the fair with a bag full of cheap baubles she'd never use." — trinkets with no real value.
  • "The children spent the afternoon hanging red and gold baubles on the Christmas tree." — tree ornaments.
  • "The king dismissed the jester, who juggled his bauble and somersaulted out of the hall." — the jester's mock-scepter.
  • "He called the trophy a bauble — a hollow reward for a meaningless competition." — figurative use, suggesting something is trivial despite appearing impressive.

If you can only hold on to one idea, hold on to this: a bauble is something small, shiny, and decorative that looks more valuable or important than it actually is. Whether it's a cheap ornament, a Christmas ball, or anything else you want to call trivial — the word always carries that same undercurrent: pretty, but not worth much.
